summary: For NASA’s "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map" challenge, the team "Poli-Nautas16" from CECyT 16 developed ARES-NAV, a decentralized web application designed to optimize missions within the Jezero crater on Mars. The system enables real-time monitoring of an astronaut’s physical condition, the plotting of safe routes, the calculation of required resources, and the management of emergency evacuations in the event of equipment failure or changing weather conditions. To achieve this, the team implemented a 100% local, "offline-first" architecture based on open web technologies (WebGL, Canvas, and JavaScript). This architecture integrates real NASA data—such as MOLA topography and mineralogical models from the Mars 2020 mission—with a modular life-support interface (comprising a "SuitHUDOverlay" and a "TelemetryPanel"). The significance of this solution lies in its comprehensive approach to balancing the critical trade-off between scientific exploration and crew safety. By operating independently of external servers, the system ensures the physical safety of personnel in hostile environments and maximizes research productivity, while also offering significant potential for adaptation to rescue operations here on Earth.
details:
Ares-Nav: Intelligent Mapping Platform for Human Exploration on Mars. Developed by the Poli-Nautas 16 team (IPN - CECyT 16 Hidalgo) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. 1. Project Overview: Ares-Nav is an intelligent, interactive mapping and navigation system designed to optimize and ensure the safety of human extravehicular activities (EVAs) on the Martian surface, using the Jezero crater—a current site of exploration—as a reference. The platform addresses the fundamental tension between maximizing scientific discovery and ensuring crew survival in a hostile environment, while accounting for communication latency with Earth (ranging from 4 to 24 minutes).

2. Core Innovation & Technological Pillars

The platform integrates planetary science, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and biomedical life-support monitoring under three foundational pillars:

  • Multilayer Geospatial Mapping: Fuses high-resolution optical imagery from HiRISE (25 cm/pixel), digital elevation models from MOLA, spectrometric mineral data from CRISM (to identify hydrated minerals, clays, and sulfates indicating aqueous environments of the past), and radiation datasets from missions like Mars 2020 (Perseverance), Curiosity, MRO, and Mars Odyssey.
  • Algorithmic Risk Matrix & Smart Routing: Proactively analyzes environmental conditions and geological hazards to calculate safe exploration routes, avoiding extreme slopes exceeding 20°–25°, loose dunes, and hazardous boulder fields.
  • Life-Support & Consumables Management: Continuously tracks critical metabolic and suit variables—including internal suit pressure (4.30 psid), carbon dioxide thresholds , oxygen consumption, hydration requirements, heart rate, and radiation accumulation ( 0.24 mSv/h)—to ensure biological viability across every sol.

3. Dual-Interface Architecture

Ares-Nav bridges planetary-scale planning and real-time execution through an integrated dual interface:

  • Habitat View (Planning Station): A desktop interface utilized prior to EVAs to map waypoints, review elevation profiles, evaluate the Global EVA Safety Index, and calculate habitat consumables relative to crew size and duration.
  • Suit View (Helmet Head-Up Display / HUD): A transparent screen projected directly onto the astronaut's helmet visor, displaying continuous biomedical telemetry and real-time visual hazard alerts so explorers can navigate autonomously without taking their eyes off the terrain

4. Methodology & Tactical Validation

The system's development follows a rigorous, multi-phase operational framework:

  1. Documentary Research & Standards: Alignment with human spaceflight standards such as NASA-STD-3001 and mission parameters.
  2. Study Area Selection & Zoning: Delineation of Jezero Crater topography and establishment of hazard zones (Z1–Z5).
  3. Data Collection & GIS Integration: Structuring multilayer orbital datasets into an accessible architectural core.
  4. Prototype Design & Simulation: Testing accelerated operational scenarios (such as 240x speed testing, emergency return protocols, and hazard-avoidance verification).
  5. Usability Analysis & Field Validation: Evaluating interface clarity to minimize astronaut cognitive load during complex surface operations.
